          // the raised median: kerbed, grassed, with a barrier down the middle
          box(x1 - x0, 0.22, median + 0.6, concMat(1, { color: 0x8a877f }), (x0 + x1) / 2, 0.11, z, "median kerb");
          box(x1 - x0 - 4, 0.30, median - 0.2, concMat(1, { color: 0x4a5a34 }), (x0 + x1) / 2, 0.30, z, "median planting");
          const rail = concMat(1, { color: 0x9aa0a6, metalness: 0.75, roughness: 0.45 });
          for (let x = x0 + 6; x < x1 - 6; x += 8) {
            box(0.16, 0.75, 0.16, rail, x, 0.72, z, "median barrier post");
          }
          box(x1 - x0 - 12, 0.34, 0.12, rail, (x0 + x1) / 2, 0.95, z, "median barrier rail");
      
          // The paint. `M.roadway` draws the whole cross-section itself — edge line,
          // lane divider, and a solid line down the middle of a divided road — from a
          // centreline and a lane count, which is the same call US-167 makes. Each
          // carriageway is therefore its own two-lane roadway, offset either side of
          // the median: without these the widest road in the game reads as a runway,
          // which is the other thing the screenshot showed.
          const laneCentre = (dir) => z + dir * (inner + laneWidth);   // the middle of the two lanes
          for (const dir of [-1, 1]) {
            M.roadway({
              lanes: lanes / 2, median: 0, laneWidth,
              points: [[x0, laneCentre(dir)], [x1, laneCentre(dir)]],
              y: 0.02,
            });
          }
      
          // shoulders, slightly different surface so the road has an edge to read
          const sh = concMat(1, { color: 0x6f6c66, roughness: 0.96 });
          for (const dir of [-1, 1]) {
            plane(x1 - x0, shoulder, sh, (x0 + x1) / 2, 0.016, z + dir * (inner + half + shoulder / 2));
          }
      
          // blockers down both outer edges: you cannot drive off the side of the
          // world's biggest road
          for (const dir of [-1, 1]) {
            const ex = z + dir * (inner + half + shoulder);
            for (let x = x0; x <= x1; x += 4) addBlocker(x, ex, 0.7);
          }
      
          // lighting, on the outside of the carriageways, alternating sides the way a
          // real arterial does so the light does not all come from one kerb
          for (let x = x0 + 20; x < x1; x += 44) {
            const dir = ((x / 44) | 0) % 2 ? 1 : -1;
            const lx = x, lz = z + dir * (pave + 1.4);
            addLitSpot({ x: lx, y: 9, z: lz, warm: 0xffd9a0, power: 150, range: 34, pole: true });
            // the pole itself, so the light has a source
            box(0.22, 9, 0.22, concMat(1, { color: 0x4a4740 }), lx, 4.5, lz, "highway light pole");
            box(1.6, 0.14, 0.3, concMat(1, { color: 0x3a3833 }), lx, 8.9, lz + dir * 0.7, "highway light arm");
          }
      
          // signage at the city end: this is the road out, and it says so
          makeBillboard(EAST_HWY.x0 + 26, 7.5, EAST_HWY.z - EAST_HALF - 5, Math.PI / 2, "EAST  ·  US-11", "CAUSEWAY  12 mi   ·   PARISH  40 mi", "THE CITY STOPS HERE. THE ROAD DOESN'T.");
        }
      
        // ---------------------------------------------------------------- the ramps
        /**
         * The ramps are what make it a road rather than a runway: a highway that
         * starts in the middle of a field cannot be entered or left, and a city with
         * no way out of it is a diorama. Each is a wedge of tarmac from the last
         * avenue up (or down) to the carriageway, with a barrier on the outside.
         */
        /**
         * A strip of tarmac running from one point to another — the primitive every
         * ramp is made of. Built as a row of quads rather than one rotated plane so
         * a curve is a curve and not a polygon with a visible corner in it.
         *
         * `channel` is the fraction of the run over which the sides are blocked in,
         * as [from, to] along the strip. It is deliberately not the whole run: a
         * ramp's merge end is INSIDE the carriageway it joins, and a channel wall
         * carried that far puts a row of blockers across the running lane of the
         * biggest road in the game. An off-ramp has the same problem at the OTHER
         * end, which is why this is a range and not a single number.
         */
        function strip(from, to, width, mat, name = "ramp", y = 0.028, channel = [0, 1]) {
          const dx = to[0] - from[0], dz = to[1] - from[1];
          const len = Math.hypot(dx, dz);
          if (len < 0.5) return [];
          const STEPS = Math.max(6, Math.round(len / 6));
          const out = [];
          for (let i = 0; i < STEPS; i++) {
            const t0 = i / STEPS, t1 = (i + 1) / STEPS;
            const ax = from[0] + dx * t0, az = from[1] + dz * t0;
            const bx = from[0] + dx * t1, bz = from[1] + dz * t1;
            const segLen = Math.hypot(bx - ax, bz - az);
            const g = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(segLen * 1.06, width, 1, 1);
            g.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
            const m = new THREE.Mesh(g, mat);
            m.position.set((ax + bx) / 2, y, (az + bz) / 2);
            // face along the segment
            m.rotation.y = -Math.atan2(bz - az, bx - ax);
            m.receiveShadow = true;
            m.name = name;
            root.add(m);
            out.push(m);
            // blockers either side, so the ramp is a channel you drive down rather
            // than a stripe you can drive across — but only over `channel`
            const mid = (t0 + t1) / 2;
            if (mid >= channel[0] && mid <= channel[1]) {
              const px = -(bz - az) / segLen, pz = (bx - ax) / segLen;
              addBlocker((ax + bx) / 2 + px * width / 2, (az + bz) / 2 + pz * width / 2, 0.7);
              addBlocker((ax + bx) / 2 - px * width / 2, (az + bz) / 2 - pz * width / 2, 0.7);
            }
          }
          return out;
        }
      
        /**
         * How far along `from -> to` the line stays more than `clear` metres from
         * z = `roadZ`. A ramp's channel walls may only exist inside that range:
         * outside it, a wall is standing in the running lane of the road the ramp is
         * joining, and no car gets past it.
         */
        function clearOf(from, to, roadZ, clear) {
          const dx = to[0] - from[0], dz = to[1] - from[1];
          for (let t = 0; t <= 1.0001; t += 0.01) {
            const z = from[1] + dz * t;
            if (Math.abs(z - roadZ) < clear) return Math.max(0, t - 0.02);
          }
          return 1;
        }
      
        /**
         * The slip roads. These are the difference between a road and a runway: a
         * highway that begins at the edge of a city with nothing joining it up cannot
         * be entered or left, and a city you cannot drive out of is a diorama.
         *
         * Two on-ramps off the cross streets and two off-ramps back down, each a
         * curve from a city street onto the correct carriageway — north side of the
         * road for eastbound, south for westbound, which is right-hand traffic and is

        function buildRamps() {
          const { x0, x1, z, lanes, median, laneWidth, shoulder } = EAST_HWY;
          const half = lanes * laneWidth / 2;
          const inner = median / 2;
          const tarmac = concMat(1, { color: 0x2e2e33, roughness: 0.94 });
          const W = 6.4;
          // the two cross streets the ramps come off, and the x they start from
          const joins = [
            { z: 370, dir: 1 },      // north cross street → eastbound (north carriageway)
            { z: 330, dir: -1 },     // south cross street → westbound (south carriageway)
          ];
          for (const j of joins) {
            const laneZ = z + j.dir * (inner + laneWidth * 0.5);   // merge into the inner lane
            // starts on the city street, curves out and joins the carriageway
            const from = [x0 - 30, j.z];
            const to = [x0 + 110, laneZ];
            // The channel stops where the ramp is still clearly OUTSIDE the
            // carriageway. The band is measured, not guessed: the ramp is 6.4 m wide,
            // so its wall has to be more than half a carriageway away from the
            // centreline before it is allowed to exist, and this loop finds that
            // point on the actual line rather than picking a fraction of it.
            // The clearance is the ramp's own half-width PLUS the carriageway's half
            // plus a margin — the wall is W/2 off the ramp's centreline, and it is
            // only "clear of the road" once that wall is outside the carriageway's
            // own half-width. Measuring the ramp CENTRE against the centreline is the
            // version that leaves a row of bollards in the running lane.
            const clear = W / 2 + half + 1.5;
            strip(from, to, W, tarmac, "on-ramp", 0.028, [0, clearOf(from, to, z, clear)]);
            // the merge nose: a gore triangle of paint where the two surfaces meet
            M.roadway({
              lanes: 1, median: 0, laneWidth: W,
              points: [[from[0], from[1]], [to[0], to[1]]],
              y: 0.03,
            });
            // a sign, because a slip road with no sign is how you end up on one
            makeBillboard(from[0] - 16, 6.5, from[1] + j.dir * 7, 0, "EAST  US-11", "KEEP RIGHT", "THE ROAD OUT");
          }
          // and the off-ramps, on the far side of the same junction
          for (const j of joins) {
            const laneZ = z + j.dir * (inner + laneWidth * 1.5);   // the OUTER lane, so you can leave
            const from = [x0 + 190, laneZ];
            const to = [x0 + 70, j.z];
            // ...and the off-ramp's channel starts at the same kind of measured
            // point, for the same reason
            const clear2 = W / 2 + half + 1.5;
            strip(from, to, W, tarmac, "off-ramp", 0.028, [1 - clearOf(from, to, z, clear2), 1]);
          }
        }
      
        // ---------------------------------------------------------------- the overpass
        /**
         * The crossing at z = 172, finished.
         *
         * It was one 150 × 1.2 × 9 m box. What made it read as unfinished from the
         * ground was not its size but its EDGES: a raw box has no parapet, so you
         * can see the deck is a slab; it has no surface, so from the approach — which
         * is the only angle anyone gets — it is untextured concrete. And it has no
         * ramp, so it is a ledge.
         */
        function buildOverpass() {
          const z = 172, y = 8, len = 150, deckW = 9;
          const tarmac = concMat(1, { color: 0x2a2a2e, roughness: 0.93 });
          const barrier = concMat(1, { color: 0xa8a49c, metalness: 0.3, roughness: 0.6 });
      
          // the deck: tarmac ON TOP of the structure, which is the part that was
          // missing. This is the surface you actually see.
          plane(len, deckW - 1.6, tarmac, 0, y + 0.62, z);
          // the kerb, either side of the running surface
          for (const s of [-1, 1]) {
            box(len, 0.28, 0.5, concMat(1, { color: 0x8f8c86 }), 0, y + 0.72, z + s * (deckW / 2 - 0.35), "overpass kerb");
          }
          // a crash barrier down each side — the thing that makes it a road
          for (const s of [-1, 1]) {
            box(len, 0.85, 0.3, barrier, 0, y + 1.25, z + s * (deckW / 2 - 0.15), "overpass parapet");
            for (let x = -len / 2 + 2; x < len / 2; x += 4) {
              box(0.14, 0.9, 0.14, barrier, x, y + 1.2, z + s * (deckW / 2 - 0.15), "parapet post");
            }
            // solid for walkers and cars, so nobody drives off the edge
            for (let x = -len / 2; x <= len / 2; x += 4) addBlocker(x, z + s * (deckW / 2), 0.8);
          }
          // lane markings along the deck: a two-lane one-way carriageway, which is
          // what the deck actually is, sitting on the structure's own height
          M.roadway({
            lanes: 2, median: 0, laneWidth: 2.4,
            points: [[-len / 2 + 2, z], [len / 2 - 2, z]],
            y: y + 0.62,
          });
      
          // Ramps at both ends, so it can be driven onto and off. Same primitive as
          // the slip roads, but with a drop: each segment sits lower than the last,
          // which is what turns a ledge into a road you can actually get up.
          for (const s of [-1, 1]) {
            const rx = s * (len / 2);
            const RUN = 34;
            const STEPS = 12;
            for (let i = 0; i < STEPS; i++) {
              const t0 = i / STEPS, t1 = (i + 1) / STEPS;
              const xa = rx + s * RUN * t0, xb = rx + s * RUN * t1;
              const w = deckW - 1.6;
              const g = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(Math.abs(xb - xa) * 1.08, w, 1, 1);
              g.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
              const m = new THREE.Mesh(g, tarmac);
              // the fall starts gentle and steepens, so the join to the deck is level
              const yHere = y + 0.62 - RAMP_RISE * Math.pow(t1, 1.4);
              m.position.set((xa + xb) / 2, yHere, z);
              // tilt to match the gradient of this segment
              const slope = (RAMP_RISE * 1.4 * Math.pow(t1, 0.4)) / RUN;
              m.rotation.z = s * Math.atan(slope);
              m.receiveShadow = true;
              m.name = "overpass ramp";
              root.add(m);
            }
            // a landing where the ramp meets the ground
            plane(12, deckW - 1.6, tarmac, rx + s * (RUN + 6), 0.03, z);
          }
        }
      
        // ---------------------------------------------------------------- build
        function build() {
          buildEastHighway();
          buildRamps();
          buildOverpass();
          root.traverse((o) => { if (o.isMesh) o.userData.noBatch = true; });
          // the paint is its own geometry, added straight to the scene by the caller
          return root;
        }
      
        return {
          root, M, build, EAST_HWY, EAST_HALF,
          get props() { return moving; },
          /** Flush the queued paint into the scene once the group is in the world. */
          flushMarkings(scene) { if (ownsMarkings) M.flush(scene); },
        };
      }
      
      export default createOrleaFringe;

      export function batchStatic(scene, opts = {}) {
        const cell = opts.cell || 48;
        const exclude = opts.exclude || (() => false);
        // A boundary owns its contents: a culling group that hides itself (composer
        // clusters) must keep its meshes, so a batch inside one is added to it rather
        // than to the scene. Everything else still merges across the scene as before.
        const boundary = opts.boundary || (() => false);
        const groups = new Map();
        const shared = new Map();          // signature -> the one material instance a batch uses
        const center = new THREE.Vector3();
        let seen = 0;
        scene.updateMatrixWorld(true);
      
        for (const root of scene.children) {
          if (!root.visible || exclude(root) || (opts.include && !opts.include(root))) continue;
          root.traverse((o) => {
            if (!o.isMesh || o.isInstancedMesh || o.isSkinnedMesh) return;
            const m = o.material;
            if (!m || Array.isArray(m) || m.isShaderMaterial) return;
            if (m.userData.surfaceKind === "asphalt" || o.userData.noBatch) return;
            for (let p = o; p; p = p.parent) if (!p.visible) return;
            if (o.matrixWorld.determinant() < 0) return;  // mirrored: winding would flip
            seen++;
            if (!o.geometry.boundingSphere) o.geometry.computeBoundingSphere();
            center.copy(o.geometry.boundingSphere.center).applyMatrix4(o.matrixWorld);
            let parent = scene;
            for (let a = o.parent; a && a !== scene; a = a.parent) if (boundary(a)) { parent = a; break; }
            const sig = matSignature(m);
            if (!shared.has(sig)) shared.set(sig, m);
            // small things (a can, a book, a fence rail) stop casting shadows: a shadow of a 30 cm object is a few pixels, and ~2,000 casters were
            // drawn into the shadow map every frame. Batches keep the flag of what they hold, so this also lets the small ones merge apart from the big.
            const sc = o.matrixWorld.getMaxScaleOnAxis();
            const cast = o.castShadow && (opts.minShadowRadius == null || o.geometry.boundingSphere.radius * sc >= opts.minShadowRadius);
            const key = [sig, attrKey(o.geometry), cast, o.receiveShadow, o.renderOrder,
              parent.id, Math.floor(center.x / cell), Math.floor(center.z / cell)].join("|");
            let g = groups.get(key);
            if (!g) groups.set(key, (g = { material: shared.get(sig), parent, template: o, cast, entries: [] }));
            g.entries.push({ mesh: o, geo: null });
          });

> So `noBatch = true` means these meshes stay individual draw calls. The blanket noBatch in the fringe's build() makes the whole fringe unbatched. That was presumably deliberate (so the fringe can be culled/hidden as a unit, or because the road planes use textures whose repeat is per-mesh and merging would break the UV repeat).
> 
> Actually: merging geometries with different texture repeats breaks the tiling. The road planes set `mat.map.repeat` per-carriageway. If merged, the repeat applies to the merged geometry's UVs — could be wrong. That's probably why.
> 
> But my new edge-strip geometry is all boxes with per-mesh materials created via `concMat(rep)` — the SAME material instance for many boxes (grassMat, etc.). Merging those is safe and correct (same material, unit-ish UVs — boxes have UVs 0..1 per face, so a merged batch would have each box's texture stretched over its own face — that's actually how it already renders, so merging is identical).

  content: |
         * ramp is made of. Built as a row of quads rather than one rotated plane so
         * a curve is a curve and not a polygon with a visible corner in it.
         *
         * `channel` is the fraction of the run over which the sides are blocked in,
         * as [from, to] along the strip. It is deliberately not the whole run: a
         * ramp's merge end is INSIDE the carriageway it joins, and a channel wall
         * carried that far puts a row of blockers across the running lane of the
         * biggest road in the game. An off-ramp has the same problem at the OTHER
         * end, which is why this is a range and not a single number.
         */
        function strip(from, to, width, mat, name = "ramp", y = 0.028, channel = [0, 1]) {
          const dx = to[0] - from[0], dz = to[1] - from[1];
          const len = Math.hypot(dx, dz);
          if (len < 0.5) return [];
          const STEPS = Math.max(6, Math.round(len / 6));
          const out = [];
          for (let i = 0; i < STEPS; i++) {
            const t0 = i / STEPS, t1 = (i + 1) / STEPS;
            const ax = from[0] + dx * t0, az = from[1] + dz * t0;
            const bx = from[0] + dx * t1, bz = from[1] + dz * t1;
            const segLen = Math.hypot(bx - ax, bz - az);
            const g = new THREE.PlaneGeometry(segLen * 1.06, width, 1, 1);
            g.rotateX(-Math.PI / 2);
            const m = new THREE.Mesh(g, mat);
            m.position.set((ax + bx) / 2, y, (az + bz) / 2);
            // face along the segment
            m.rotation.y = -Math.atan2(bz - az, bx - ax);        m.receiveShadow = true;
              m.name = name;
              out.add(m);
              out.push(m);
            // blockers either side, so the ramp is a channel you drive down rather
            // than a stripe you can drive across — but only over `channel`
            const mid = (t0 + t1) / 2;
            if (mid >= channel[0] && mid <= channel[1]) {
              const px = -(bz - az) / segLen, pz = (bx - ax) / segLen;
              addBlocker((ax + bx) / 2 + px * width / 2, (az + bz) / 2 + pz * width / 2, 0.7);
              addBlocker((ax + bx) / 2 - px * width / 2, (az + bz) / 2 - pz * width / 2, 0.7);
            }
          }
          return out;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// crowd.js — the people: who is in the room, and who is on the pavement.
//
// A venue's fixtures know where a bar is, where the machines face and which way
// the stage looks, so they are what proposes *people*: `b.spot(lx, lz, { role })`
// next to their own geometry (interiors.js). This module turns that list of
// candidates into actors — nobody is placed by hand, and a floor plan that moves
// a bar moves its barman with it.
//
// Three rules, all of them about not being the most expensive thing on screen:
//
//   * The roles are `characters.js`'s own procedural people. No skinning, no
//     AnimationMixer, no new assets.
//   * The *mix* is spawnzones.js's `entertainment` table — the same weights that
//     already decide who walks the strip when the player is not looking. A room
//     full of patrons is therefore a room full of the Crown Strip's own crowd,
//     not a second casting decision that could drift from it.
//   * The actors carry `userData.noBatch`, so merge.js's batch sweep leaves them
//     alone: a merged actor is an actor that can never dance again. Everything
//     else about them is cheap — one beat per actor, decided on staggered
//     timers, and the district only ticks the groups it has made visible.
//
// Beats, and nothing more: `still` (standing where the fixture wanted them),
// `shuffle` (a step inside a small radius — the dance floor and the sidewalk),
// `stroll` (walking a lane the district has checked is clear), `work` (a shift at
// a station — HAPPY HOGS' barman cycles pour/polish/serve/lean along his counter),
// and `act` (a scripted performance, and there is only ever one). A strolling actor
// is why walk lanes are picked against the venue's own collision.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

import * as THREE from "three";
import { ZONE_MIX } from "./spawnzones.js";
import {
  makeStripper, makeHog, makeStar, randomGayMan, randomHighEndEscort, randomHoodrat,
  randomLesbian, randomProstitute, randomRedneck, randomTuxedo,
} from "./characters.js";

function mulberry(a) {
  return function () {
    a |= 0; a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let q = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a);
    q = (q + Math.imul(q ^ (q >>> 7), 61 | q)) ^ q;
    return ((q ^ (q >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296;
  };
}

/**
 * The kinds of person the strip draws, and the factory each one comes from.
 * Heights mirror main.js's ENEMY_TYPES so the man who walked in off the avenue
 * and the man standing inside the door are the same size.
 *
 * `tourist` and `suit` have no 3D factory of their own — main.js spawns those as
 * billboards — so on the strip they wear the dinner jacket. Noted rather than
 * hidden: they are the two kinds that do not look exactly like their outside
 * counterpart.
 */
const KIND_FACTORY = {
  tuxedo:        { h: 1.86, make: randomTuxedo },
  tourist:       { h: 1.85, make: randomTuxedo },
  hoodrat:       { h: 1.92, make: randomHoodrat },
  thug:          { h: 1.98, make: randomHoodrat },
  highendescort: { h: 1.82, make: randomHighEndEscort },
  prostitute:    { h: 1.80, make: randomProstitute },
  gayman:        { h: 1.86, make: randomGayMan },
  lesbian:       { h: 1.78, make: randomLesbian },
  suit:          { h: 1.90, make: randomTuxedo },
  redneck:       { h: 2.00, make: randomRedneck },
};

/** Who the strip draws when a spot has no opinion: spawnzones.js's door mix. */

      export function makeCrowd(spots, o = {}) {
        const rng = mulberry((o.seed | 0) || 7);
        const group = new THREE.Group();
        const chosen = selectSpots(spots, { count: o.count ?? 12, rng, minGap: o.minGap });
        const actors = [];
        let meshes = 0;
      
        for (const s of chosen) {
          const role = roleOf(s.role);
          const a = role.mix ? makeMixed(rng, s.scale || 1) : role.make(rng, (role.h || 1.84) * (s.scale || 1), s);
          if (s.name) a.userData.name = s.name;
          place(a, s, role, rng);
          const beat = s.beat || role.beat || "still";
          const rec = {
            a, beat, anim: s.anim || role.anim || "idle",
            home: new THREE.Vector3(s.lx, s.y || 0, s.lz),
            radius: s.r ?? role.r ?? 0.9,
            goal: new THREE.Vector3(s.lx, s.y || 0, s.lz),
            lane: s.lane ? o.lane : null,
            end: null, wait: rng() * 3, speed: s.speed ?? (0.9 + rng() * 0.35),
            role: s.role || "patron",
            // the front row of a stage: `hype` marks somebody who is watching the act
            // rather than the room, so a big move reaches them and not the whole bar
            hype: 0, fan: !!s.hype,
            // a scripted actor's stage, if its fixture staged one
            bounds: s.bounds,
            // the bar shift, for the `work` beat: which poses, and which way the
            // counter runs (`patrol`), so his steps go along the bar and not into it
            poses: s.poses || role.poses || BAR_POSES,
            pose: 0,
            patrol: s.patrol || null,
            // the facing the part was cast at, for beats that move an actor who is not
            // supposed to turn with its feet (a barman walking his counter)
            face: s.face != null ? s.face : a._yaw,
            // main.js's fire() hit-tests the room the same way it hits the street:
            // hp, a death pose, gone. The house's own hogs carry a couple more than
            // a patron — hp values mirror main.js's ENEMY_TYPES (redneck/hoodrat vs
            // hog) without importing that table, so this module stays decoupled.
            hp: a.userData.hog ? 6 : 4, dead: false,
          };
          if (beat === "stroll" && o.lane) {
            const l = o.lane;
            rec.lane = l;
            rec.home.set(s.lx, s.y || 0, l.z);
            rec.z = l.z;
            rec.end = rng() < 0.5 ? l.x0 : l.x1;
            rec.a.position.z = l.z;
          }
          a.traverse((m) => {
            if (!m.isMesh) return;
            m.userData.noBatch = true;      // an actor that gets batched can never move again
            m.userData.crowd = true;
            meshes++;
          });
          group.add(a);
          // The shift: staff hold the room all day, the people the room is *for* only
          // turn up after dark. `beat: "stroll"` (a stroller on the pavement) counts as
          // nightlife too, whatever role it was cast as.
          rec.night = !DAY_ROLES.has(rec.role) || s.night === true;
          rec.dayOk = !!s.day || DAY_ROLES.has(rec.role);

          group, actors, meshes, tick, setShift, cheerAt, scatter: (fromX, fromZ) => applyScatter(actors, fromX, fromZ, group),
          // the show, for the district to expose (and for the QA to watch run)
          act, fans,

      /**
       * Give an actor a route to walk, one leg at a time, and take it off its beat
       * until the route is done.
       *
       * @param {object} x    a record from `makeCrowd` / `makePavement` / a spare
       * @param {Array}  legs [{ x, z, wait, on, speed }] — walk here, hold `wait`
       *                      seconds playing `on`, then the next one
       * @param {Function} [done]  called when the last leg is finished (and clears it)
       */
      export function scriptActor(x, legs, done) {
        x.script = { legs, i: 0, wait: legs.length ? legs[0].wait || 0 : 0, done: done || null };
        return x.script;
      }

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// streetlife.js — the people who make a city look inhabited.
//
//   const S = createStreetLife({ scene, resolveCollision, isNight, camera })
//   S.build(routes)             routes: [{ a: [x, z], b: [x, z], kind, name }]
//   S.update(dt, playerPos)
//   S.get props()               anything that moves: main.js keeps it out of batchStatic
//
// "general city-like NPCs like businessmen and like cops patrolling streets etc"
// (human request, 2026-10-01)
//
// The city grew from four hundred and sixty-five blocks of new building with
// nobody in any of it. Traffic makes a road look used; it does not make a
// street look like a street. What makes a city read as inhabited is PEOPLE on
// the PAVEMENT — walking it, waiting at it, working it — and this is the
// cheapest and largest win available, because these are the same rigs the rest
// of the game already casts.
//
// Two kinds, and they are different in kind rather than in colour:
//
//   commuter  an office worker crossing the city on the way to or from work.
//              Daytime only, quick, purposeful, in a suit. They are the reason a
//              CBD looks open at nine in the morning.
//   beat      a policeman walking a fixed route. ALWAYS there, day or night —
//              which is what makes a city feel policed, and is the thing the
//              existing foot-cop system could never do: it only spawns a
//              deputy in response to the player being wanted, so an empty street
//              and a street under martial law looked identical.
//
// Everything is distance-culled. A person 200 m away is not drawn, not updated
// and not collided, and the pool is capped, so the cost of a big city is
// bounded by how much of it you can see rather than by how much of it exists.

        /**
         * May an adult clip play on this actor? Two independent conditions, both
         * required: the rig knows how old this character is and it is past the floor,
         * AND the 18+ gate has been answered at the door. A caller cannot skip this by
         * setting `anim` directly — `play()` is the only way a clip is entered, and it
         * checks.
         */
        allowsAdultClip() {
          const age = this.userData && this.userData.age;
          if (typeof age !== "number" || !(age >= ADULT_CLIP_MIN_AGE)) return false;
          return typeof adultGate === "function" && adultGate() === true;
        }
      
        play(anim, { loop = true, force = false } = {}) {
          if (ADULT_CLIPS.has(anim) && !this.allowsAdultClip()) {
            // Fail closed and say so. An adult clip on an actor whose age is
            // unverified, or before the 18+ gate has been answered, is refused here
            // rather than trusted to every call site to have checked — the gate is a
            // property of the rig, not of the venue that happens to be casting.
            this.adultClipRefused = anim;
            return;
          }
          this.adultClipRefused = null;
          if (this.anim === anim && !force) return;
          this.anim = anim;
          this.loop = loop;
          this.time = 0;
          this.finished = false;
          if (anim === "death") this._deathKind = undefined;
        }
      
        update(dt) {
          this.time += dt;
      
          // measure our own travel so the gait matches the actual ground speed and
          // we face the way we are going — no changes needed in updateEnemy()
          const dx = this.position.x - this._last.x;
          const dz = this.position.z - this._last.z;
          const moved = Math.hypot(dx, dz);
          this._speed = dt > 0 ? moved / dt : 0;
          if (moved > 1e-4) {
            const want = Math.atan2(dx, dz);
            let d = want - this._yaw;
            while (d > Math.PI) d -= Math.PI * 2;
            while (d < -Math.PI) d += Math.PI * 2;
            this._yaw += d * Math.min(1, dt * 9);

          // ---- what the character is holding ----------------------------------
          // Runs AFTER the clip, never instead of it: walking, running and the dance
          // clips still drive the legs, hips and torso, and only the arms are taken
          // over so the weapon is held. This is the hook that makes a weapon part of
          // the character instead of a prop parked beside it.
          if (this.weaponHold) this.applyWeaponHold(dt);
        }
      
        /**
         * Every animation clip, one branch per `this.anim` — unchanged. Split out of
         * update() so the weapon hold can be layered on top of whatever pose the clip
         * produced, including the clips that return early.
         */
        _poseClip(dt) {
          const A = this.arms, L = this.legs;
      
          if (this.anim === "death") {
            // Nobody falls the same way twice: onto a side, backwards, or forwards onto the face — chosen once per body from its
            // own seed, and mirrored for the side fall. `finished` gates the fade in updateEnemy.
            // A hit lands first (the torso snaps back for a tenth of a second), the fall accelerates (ease-in, like a body, not a
            // door), the impact overshoots a hair and settles, and the corpse RESTS on the ground: the body pivots about its feet,

      /** Who the strip draws when a spot has no opinion: spawnzones.js's door mix. */
      const DOOR_MIX = ZONE_MIX.entertainment;
      
      /**
       * A weighted bag built from that mix, so `ZONE_MIX.entertainment` stays the only
       * place the strip's crowd is described. Any kind without a factory here simply
       * does not appear (there is no hobo on the strip's door list, and no hog).
       */
      function buildBag(mix) {
        const bag = [];
        for (const [kind, weight] of Object.entries(mix)) {
          if (kind === "border" || !KIND_FACTORY[kind]) continue;
          for (let i = 0; i < Math.round(weight * 100); i++) bag.push(kind);
        }
        return bag.length ? bag : ["tuxedo"];
      }
      const BAG = buildBag(DOOR_MIX);
      
      /** Somebody off that bag, at the height the spawn tables use for their kind. */
      function makeMixed(rng, scale = 1) {
        const kind = BAG[(rng() * BAG.length) | 0];
        const { h, make } = KIND_FACTORY[kind];
        const a = make(rng, h * scale);
        a.userData.crowdKind = kind;
        return a;
      }
      
      /**
       * The bar shift, in order: pour, wipe down, hand it over, lean and watch the
       * room, breathe. Four poses plus idle, shuffled by the beat, is enough that the
       * counter never settles into a loop you can read from the door.
       */
      const BAR_POSES = ["pour", "polish", "serve", "barlean", "idle", "pour", "barlean"];
      
      /**
       * The casting sheet. A fixture's `role` hint is a *staff* part (somebody has to
       * be behind the bar); anything unhinted is drawn from the door mix.
       *
       * `beat` is what the actor does with its time, `anim` the clip it holds while
       * standing. Only ever clips characters.js already has.
       */
      export const ROLES = {
        // ---- staff: pinned by whichever fixture owns that part of the room --------
        barkeep:   { anim: "idle",  h: 1.88, make: (r, h) => randomHoodrat(r, h) },
        dealer:    { anim: "idle",  h: 1.86, make: (r, h) => randomTuxedo(r, h) },

       *
       * @param {Array<{lx:number, lz:number, role?:string}>} spots
       * @param {{count:number, rng:Function, minGap?:number}} o
       */
      export function selectSpots(spots, { count = 12, rng = Math.random, minGap = 1.5 } = {}) {
        // staff first, so a bar full of stools cannot crowd the barman out of his job
        const chosen = spots.filter((s) => s.role && ROLES[s.role]);
        const free = spots.filter((s) => !s.role);
        for (let i = free.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {           // deterministic shuffle
          const j = (rng() * (i + 1)) | 0;
          [free[i], free[j]] = [free[j], free[i]];
        }
        // two passes: spread properly first, then relax the gap to reach `count` in a
        // small room (a DJ booth's three spots are all inside 2 m of each other)
        for (const gap of [minGap, minGap * 0.55]) {
          for (const s of free) {
            if (chosen.length >= count) break;
            if (chosen.some((c) => Math.hypot(c.lx - s.lx, c.lz - s.lz) < gap)) continue;
            chosen.push(s);
          }
        }
        return chosen.slice(0, count);
      }
      
      /** Place one actor at a local spot and give it its beat. */
      function place(a, s, role, rng) {
        a.position.set(s.lx, s.y || 0, s.lz);
        a.baseY = s.y || 0;
        const yaw = s.face != null ? s.face : rng() * Math.PI * 2;
        a._yaw = yaw;
        a.rotation.y = yaw;
        if (a._last) a._last.copy(a.position);
        // a spot may name its own pose (a fan zone dancing, a stool-punter slouched):
        // the role's default is for the part, the spot's is for this ten square metres
        a.play(s.anim || role.anim || "idle", { force: true, loop: true });
        a.update(0.001);                 // settle the first pose out of the bind pose
      }
      
      // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
      // The act — BILLY JEANS, on the lounge's stage.

      const peds = [];
      function loadPed(name, x, z) {
        const tex = texLoader.load(`./assets/models/trailerpark/chars/${name}.png`);
        tex.colorSpace = THREE.SRGBColorSpace; tex.flipY = false;
        fbxLoader.load(`./assets/models/trailerpark/chars/${name}.fbx`, (obj) => {
          const sz = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(obj).getSize(new THREE.Vector3());
          obj.scale.setScalar(1.9 / (sz.y || 1.9));
          obj.traverse((o) => {
            if (o.isMesh) { o.castShadow = true; o.material = new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ map: tex, roughness: 0.9 }); }
          });
          const b = new THREE.Box3().setFromObject(obj);
          obj.position.set(x, -b.min.y, z);
          obj.rotation.y = Math.random() * 6;
          scene.add(obj);
          peds.push(obj);
          addBlocker(x, z, 0.5);
        }, undefined, () => {});
      }
      
      function buildShack(wall, doorway, windowW, roofC, cx, cz, rot) {
        const g = new THREE.Group();
        g.position.set(cx, 0, cz);
        g.rotation.y = rot;
        scene.add(g);
        const put = (src, px, pz, ry) => {
          if (!src) return;
          const o = src.clone(true);
          o.position.set(px, 0, pz); o.rotation.y = ry;
          g.add(o);
        };
        const W = 4;
        put(doorway, 0, W / 2, 0);
        put(windowW, -W / 2, 0, Math.PI / 2);
        put(windowW, W / 2, 0, Math.PI / 2);
        put(wall, 0, -W / 2, 0);
        if (roofC) { const r = roofC.clone(true); r.position.y = 3.0; r.scale.set(1.3, 1, 1.3); g.add(r); }
        // approximate collision as a ring of blockers
        addBlocker(cx, cz + 2, 1.4);
        addBlocker(cx, cz - 2, 1.4);

    if (z < -50 && x >= coreMinX) return "town";

I dug into this and found something real, but I also want to be straight with you: **I have not proven this is what you're looking at**, because "the old NPCs" could mean several different systems. Here's what I verified.

**It is not my last three commits.** `spawnzones.js` was last touched in `0ee4c2e`, and the `ENEMY_CAP` line was last changed in `7e2caf5` on **2026-09-14**. My work (weapons, roads, dialogue, edge strip) doesn't touch NPC spawning at all.

**But the caps predate the world by two weeks.** This is the concrete finding:

- `ENEMY_CAP = 48` living ambient NPCs, or 74 in urban/entertainment zones (`main.js:3786`)
- Anything further than **160 m** from the player is culled
- That was set on 2026-09-14. The state map was then made **5× larger**, and OrleaRouge was **doubled** on 2026-09-28.

So 48 people across a 5.76 km² state is roughly 8 people per km², and you only ever see the ones inside a 160 m bubble. The caps were never rescaled when the world grew — the traffic cap next to it even carries a comment admitting it (`maxCars: 28 // ...the state-wide map is 5x the old one; this is a density tune`), and nobody did the same for people.

**A second, sharper problem.** `spawnzones.pick()` hard-returns `null` when the player is in the city and there is no POI inside the spawn ring — there is no fallback. I built the city headlessly to count. OrleaRouge registers 140 POIs, and the ring finds a healthy 3–16 downtown. But standing at the **Crown Strip (Metro)** or anywhere on the **new east arterial**, the ring finds **zero** — so `pick()` returns null and **nothing spawns at all**, indefinitely. The strip I just built has no POIs whatsoever. That would read exactly as "everyone's gone."

**What I ruled out:** the faction war. It's capped by `npcs.hostileCount` against `MAX_HOSTILE`, and `FIGHTERS` only contains gang members — it can't grind down the crowd roles.

Author: Chimthuwu <chimske@gmail.com>

    Double the size of OrleaRouge and zone it properly
    
    656 x 186 m — about twelve blocks by four, which is a large town. It is now
    816 x 304, twice the area, and the growth is east and south because the Quarter
    and the parish are fixed by geography and a CBD is not.
    
    The four block builders used to decide what a block was with overlapping
    position tests, so a block could satisfy "downtown" and "outskirts" at once and
    whichever ran first took it. One zoneOf() now answers for all of them, and the
    sequence west to east is the sequence you drive into: Quarter, Garden District,
    downtown, midtown, the civic end, with a low-rise northern edge over the top.
    
    Two things fell out of doing it properly. The old "outskirts" zone became
    unreachable once the civic end grew out to meet it, so it was dead code that
    still read as though the city had a run-down district. And the city reached the
    Bayou State Penitentiary, which is Angola — a hundred miles from New Orleans and
    now 242 m out on Delta Road, walls, rodeo arena and all.
    
    The lanes were four hand-listed pairs at fixed offsets, which meant a street
    with no traffic on it the moment the grid grew past four. They are generated
    from the grid now.

> The density check fails at 1376/km². My upper bound of 600 was arbitrary. 156 people in a 190 m radius = 0.113 km² → 1376/km². That's very dense for an ambient crowd — honestly 156 people all within 190 m is a LOT, and it's a real draw-call risk.
> 
> Let me reconsider the numbers honestly. 190 m radius circle = π * 0.19² = 0.1134 km². 
> - Old: 48+26=74 → 652/km². 
> - New: 110+46=156 → 1376/km². Double the old density.
> 
> Is 1376/km² too much? In a real city, a busy downtown has maybe 1000-2000 people per km². 1376 is plausible for "a busy street" but at 190 m radius it means 156 visible people, which is genuinely a lot of 3D actors.
> 
> The old setting (74 within 160 m) = 74/(π*0.16²)=74/0.0804 = 920/km². So the old density was already ~920/km² in urban. The user found that too empty! So density per se isn't the issue — the issue must be that NPCs weren't SPAWNING (the pick() null), not that the cap was low.

> That's an important realization: with 74 in a 160 m ring, the street should NOT have looked empty. The real cause is more likely the pick() null (which I've fixed) — and possibly the corner-town building blackouts.
>

> _Reasoning_
> Pushed. Someone else (or a parallel agent) had pushed a commit widening US-167 — I merged it, tests still green, pushed.
> 
> Now let me report honestly. Key points:
> 1. The real cause found and fixed: pick() hard null.
> 2. I was wrong about `building` and reverted — I must say this plainly.
> 3. Caps hedged, not the main bug.
> 4. Caveat: no browser, so nobody has seen a street.
> 
> Let me be concise.

Pushed. Here's the honest version.

## The cause

`spawnzones.js` `pick()`, in its city branch:

```js
if (!spots.length) return null;
```

A **hard stop**, every tick, forever. OrleaRouge registers 140 POIs so downtown was fine — but the **Crown Strip and the new east arterial have zero POIs at any distance**, so the population tick could never produce a person there. The ring position had already been computed a few lines earlier and is a perfectly good spot; the POI snap was an *improvement*, not a precondition. It's now `if (spots.length)`.

`pickKind()` also warns once on an unknown zone name instead of returning `null` in silence — that's the failure mode that turns a district into an empty field with nothing in the logs.

## I got it wrong first, and reverted it

I diagnosed the `building` zone as an accidental leak — a composer's word with no `ZONE_MIX` entry, **0.43 km² of silent blackout** — and "fixed" it. **It is deliberate.** `composer.js:355` says so in its own docstring: *"'building' is no spawn zone: nobody appears inside walls."* `crownstrip.js` relies on the same rule. My fix would have filled four corner towns with people standing inside buildings. Reverted — `src/stateWorld.js` is byte-identical to `HEAD`. The new test now asserts `building`, `water` and `highway` are *still* empty so it can't quietly come back.

## The caps are a hedge, not the cure

`48 → 90`, downtown `+26 → +30`, cull `160 m → 180 m`. Deliberately modest, and the reasoning is written at the declaration: **48 + 26 inside a 160 m ring is already ~920 people per km²** — a crowded street, not an empty one. So the cap was never the main bug.

My first draft raised it to 110/46 at a 190 m ring, and the density check I'd just written caught it at **1376 people per km²** — paying draw calls for a mob. I backed it off rather than ship my own overcorrection.

## What I have *not* verified

**Nobody has looked at a street.** There's no Chrome on this machine, so this is entirely headless measurement. The test proves `pick()` now returns a spot at eight named places — Crown Strip 40/40, east arterial 40/40, downtown 40/40, the woods 40/40, Port Calypso only 7/40 — but "returns a spot" is not "looks populated".

Two loose ends worth your eye: **Port Calypso is the thinnest town in the state** (7/40, because `building` and `water` legitimately cover the docks), and the **Crown Strip's own pavement crowd was folded into `streetlife.js`** at some point, which may deserve casting back.

`b370248`, merged with your US-167 widening (`9235a59`) — full suite green on the merge.

> _Reasoning_
> Found the bug. In `junction()`:
> 
> ```js
> if (striped) {
>   for (const s of [1, -1]) {
>     crosswalk(x + s * (half + D.crosswalkDepth / 2 + 1.2), z, {
>       alongX: !alongX, half, stripes: 7, y0,
>     });
>   }
> }
> ```
>

**Found it — and it's a one-word bug.** The steeple "tower" is built as a **cube**, not a tower:

```js
const steeple = (x, z, height, shaft) => {
  mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(shaft, shaft, shaft), stucco, cx + x, 30 + height / 2, cz + z, ...)
```

`shaft` is the *width*; the second argument should be `height`. So the central steeple draws an 11 m **cube** sitting at y 55.5–66.5, while its spire starts at y 92 — **25.5 m of nothing between them**. The end steeples leave 14.5 m gaps. That's your floating towers, exactly.

```

It did look cool — the three-unequal-steeples silhouette is genuinely the thing that makes it *the* Cathedral rather than a church. But you photographed a real bug and I chased it down.

**One word.** In `nolalandmarks.js`:

```js
mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(shaft, shaft, shaft), stucco, cx + x, 30 + height / 2, cz + z, …)
```

`shaft` is the tower's **width**. The second argument is its **height**. So the "tower" was a *cube* of the width — while the spire above it was positioned at `30 + height + height * 0.21`, on top of where a full-height shaft would have ended.

Measured by building the block headlessly:

- Central: an 11 m **cube** at y 55.5–66.5, under a spire starting at **y 92** → **25.5 m of nothing**
- End steeples: 9 m cubes at y 44.5–53.5, spires at **y 68** → **14.5 m of nothing each**

Now `BoxGeometry(shaft, height, shaft)`, centred at `30 + height/2`, so it spans exactly `30 … 30+height` — the y the spire was already placed to sit on. Shafts measure **30→92, 30→68, 30→68**, each meeting its spire's base to the centimetre.

**The part I found more interesting: why every existing check passed.** `landmarks_test.mjs` counted three crosses, compared their heights ("central steeple much taller" — 122 m vs 87 m) and measured the whole thing over 80 m tall. All true. All green. With the towers in mid-air.

Counting can't find a gap. So the new checks measure **the joint** — for each spire, find the shaft under the same x/z, require it starts on the roofline and *ends where the spire begins*. I verified it fails **6 times** against the old code and passes on the new, so it's a guard and not a decoration.

That lesson generalises past the Cathedral: *"it built three of the right things at the right relative heights"* is not *"it is one building"*. A missing **volume between two correct, well-placed parts** survives every count and every silhouette test. Worth checking the other landmarks for the same class of seam when you get a chance — the Superdome and the Cabildo are the obvious candidates.

Pushed as `b9cfe71`, full suite green. Still open from earlier: the Crown Strip flagship back rooms (diagnosed, not built — only `franchiseClubs.js` has them, so HAPPY HOGS never had one at all), the City Park crowds, the transit system, and those mystery boxes on the US-167 centreline.

> _Reasoning_
> Interesting — the survey says almost everything is "built or paved", 0% empty. But the user says there's lots of empty space.
> 
> The problem: my classification counts ANY mesh with height > 1.2 m as "built", including a single lamp post, a fence, a tree, a car. And ANY flat mesh (h < 1.2) as "paved", including the giant ground plane and lawn.
> 
> Chatboro: 348 meshes for 0.0317 km² — that's 348 meshes over 31,700 m². And "100% built, 94.8% paved" — because the town has a giant ground plane covering everything (paved), so there's no "empty" by my definition.
> 
> So my metric is useless for the user's question. The user's complaint is about **sparse-feeling** space — big open areas between buildings, where you can see a lot of nothing. The right metric is not "is any mesh here" but **"how much of the ground within sight is building mass vs open"**.
> 
> Better metric: a cell is "urban" if a BUILDING with real footprint (> ~25 m²) and real height (> ~4 m) covers a decent fraction of it. A cell with only a lamp post or a car is effectively open.
> 
> Let me redefine:
> - For each cell, compute the fraction of the cell area covered by building footprints (meshes whose height >= 4 m and whose footprint area >= 20 m²).
> - Report the mean coverage and the cells with LOW coverage.
> - "Empty" = coverage < 10% AND no road.
> 
> Also, the real question: "concrete jungle" means TALL and DENSE. So report **mean building height** and **sky coverage** too. The best single metric for "urban feel" is probably: for each point, is there a building within 25 m? And mean height of nearby buildings.
> 
> Let me reframe: measure **built mass**: sum of (footprint area × height) per cell, i.e. a density, and compare districts. Plus mean height of the tallest building within 40 m of a sample point.
> 
> Simplest useful thing: for each district, sample points on a grid and compute:
> - `nearest building distance` (to a structure ≥4 m tall and ≥20 m² footprint)
> - mean/max height of buildings within 50 m
> Then: "how much of this district is more than 30 m from a real building".
> 
> That directly measures "empty space that could be filled up".
> 
> Let me rewrite the survey with that. This is the metric the user's request actually implies.
> 
> Let me rewrite.

My metric was useless — it counted a lamp post as "built" and a lawn as "paved", so everything read as full. The question is really *"how much open ground is there, and how tall is what's near it"*. Let me measure that instead.

a \"structure\" is >= ${MIN_FOOT} m2 footprint and >= ${MIN_H} m tall\\n`);\n  console.log(`  ${\"district\".padEnd(12)} {\"ha\":>6} {\"bldgs\":>6} {\"mass/ha\":>8} {\"medReach\":>9} {\"%>30m\":>6} {\"medH\":>5} {\"p90H\":>5} {\"maxH\":>5}`);\n  for (const r of report) {\n    console.log(`  ${r.name.padEnd(12)} ${String(r.hectares).padStart(6)} ${String(r.structures).padStart(6)} ${String(r.massPerHa).padStart(8)} ${String(r.medianReach).padStart(8)}m ${(r.over30m + \"%\").padStart(6)} ${String(r.medianHeight).padStart(4)}m ${String(r.p90Height).padStart(4)}m ${String(r.maxHeight).padStart(4)}m`);\n  }\n  console.log(`\\n  mass/ha = built footprint x height per hectare.         function buildSet() {
          // ---- what is already there, claimed before anything is composed: the highway and its roadside lots (stores, gas, the trailer park and
          // the junkyard), and Parish Highway 9 swinging away to the south-west
          C.claim({ x0: -62, x1: 52, z0: METRO_BOUNDS.z0, z1: METRO_BOUNDS.z1 });
          for (let x = -292; x < -60; x += 8) for (let z = METRO_BOUNDS.z0; z < METRO_BOUNDS.z1; z += 8) {
            if (onParishHighway(x + 4, z + 4, 30)) C.claim({ x0: x, x1: x + 8, z0: z, z1: z + 8 });
          }
      
          // ---- roads. Streets stop at the highway lots and at the outer edge; the avenues run the full depth.
          for (const z of STREETS_Z) {
            C.road(`Metro Street ${z}`, [[56, z], [280, z]], { width: STREET_W, lampEvery: 38, y: 0.021 });
            C.road(`Metro Street W ${z}`, [[-280, z], [-66, z]], { width: STREET_W, lampEvery: 38, y: 0.021 });
          }
          // sidewalk: 0.9, not composer's default 1.6. The blocks either side of an
          // avenue sit 7 m back from the centreline, and 12/2 + 1.6 = 7.6 meant the
          // claimed corridor overlapped the block by 0.6 m on every avenue — the
          // sidewalk was being drawn through the kerb of the building behind it. The
          // avenue is the widest road in the district and the one most likely to be
          // walked across, so it keeps a real footway; it just fits inside the gap.
          for (const x of AVENUES_X) C.road(`Bayou Avenue ${x}`, [[x, -120], [x, 120]], { width: AVENUE_W, sidewalk: 0.9, lampEvery: 34, y: 0.022 });
      
          // ---- the paint. Four lanes of traffic on a road with no lane markings is
          // the same invisible-work problem US-167 had: the cars are real and the
          // tarmac says nothing about them. Crossings go at the avenue/street
          // junctions and at the grid's edge, where the avenues run out of city.
          {
            const M = createMarkings({ y: 0.021 });
            for (const z of STREETS_Z) {
              M.roadway({ ...STREET_ROAD, points: [[62, z], [274, z]], y: 0.021 });
              M.roadway({ ...STREET_ROAD, points: [[-72, z], [-274, z]], y: 0.021 });
              for (const x of AVENUES_X) {
                M.junction(x, z, { alongX: true, half: STREET_W / 2, y0: 0.021 });
              }
            }
            for (const x of AVENUES_X) {
              M.roadway({ ...AVENUE_ROAD, points: [[x, 118], [x, -118]], y: 0.021 });
              // the avenue's far ends, where it leaves the grid
              for (const z of [-108, 112]) M.junction(x, z + (z < 0 ? -6 : 6), { alongX: false, half: AVENUE_W / 2, y0: 0.021 });
            }
            M.flush(scene);
          }
      
          // ---- the blocks
          let n = 0;
          for (let i = 0; i < COLS.length; i++) {
            for (let j = 0; j < ROWS.length; j++) {
              const [x0, x1] = COLS[i], [z0, z1] = ROWS[j];
              const b = { x0, x1, z0, z1, cx: (x0 + x1) / 2, cz: (z0 + z1) / 2, w: x1 - x0, d: z1 - z0 };
              if (!C.isFree({ x0: b.x0, x1: b.x1, z0: b.z0, z1: b.z1 })) {
                // the highway's exclusion clips this block: fill whichever thirds are still free with a smaller building each, so the city does not
                // stop in a ragged blank edge beside Parish Highway 9
                const third = b.w / 3;
                for (let k = 0; k < 3; k++) {
                  const sb = { x0: b.x0 + k * third + 1, x1: b.x0 + (k + 1) * third - 1, z0: b.z0, z1: b.z1 };
                  if (!C.isFree(sb)) continue;
                  const scx = (sb.x0 + sb.x1) / 2, scz = (sb.z0 + sb.z1) / 2, sw = sb.x1 - sb.x0, sd = sb.z1 - sb.z0, hh = hash(scx, scz, 11);
                  C.cluster(`partial ${n}.${k}`, () => {
                    const g = new THREE.Group(); scene.add(g);
                    if (hh < 0.45) parts.tower(g, scx, scz, Math.min(28, sw - 4), Math.min(26, sd - 8), 40 + hash(scx, scz, 12) * 44, [0, 1, 3][(n + k) % 3], n + k);
                    else if (hh < 0.75) parts.rowhouses(g, sb.x0 + 1, sb.x1 - 1, sb.z0 + 5, -1, n + k);
                    else parts.plaza(g, scx, scz, sw - 6, sd - 10, n + k);
                    if (hh >= 0.45 && hh < 0.75) parts.rowhouses(g, sb.x0 + 1, sb.x1 - 1, sb.z1 - 5, 1, n + k + 5);
                  });
                  C.claim(sb);
                }
                n++;
                continue;

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// westparish.js — the rural west: Parish Highway 9 and Bayou Noir.
//
// The map grows west from x = −136 to PARISH_MIN_X. Parish Highway 9 is a
// four-lane road built for driving fast: it leaves US-167 just south of the
// strip's middle (z ≈ 8), curves south-west through the pines, runs a long
// straight past a rest stop, swings south, and bends east into OrleaRouge on
// street 330, a second way into the city besides the causeway.
//
// Road hierarchy: US-167 (major road) → Parish Highway 9 (highway) → the dirt
// road to Bayou Noir (rural road) → OrleaRouge's street grid (local streets).
//
// Off the highway: forest (chunked instanced pines, so frustum culling still
// works), Bayou Noir (a church and general store from Buildings.glb, shacks, a
// barn, the water tower) and fenced sugar-cane fields, a rest stop with the
// gas-station asset, and swamp water in the bayou band.
//
// The route is plain data sampled at import, so keepouts (no trees on the road)
// work before anything is built. Orientation follows world.js.
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

import * as THREE from "three";
import { headingFromVector } from "./world.js";
import { makeChurch } from "./church.js";
import { makeDecorativeFence, placeParkedCar, placeGasStation } from "./landmarks.js";

export const PARISH_MIN_X = -440;
const REGION_EAST_X = -150;        // west of this is the parish proper
const WEST_ROAD_Z = 300;         // corridors.js Bayou Pines Road
export const HWY_WIDTH = 14;       // two 3.5 m lanes each way

// the highway's centreline, US-167 → OrleaRouge street 330
const CONTROL = [
  [-9, 8], [-60, 8], [-110, 14], [-150, 30], [-190, 58],
  [-260, 120], [-320, 175], [-352, 215], [-366, 260], [-362, 300],
  [-340, 328], [-300, 334], [-220, 331], [-138, 330],
];
const STEP = 4;                    // metres between samples

const toCurve = (pts) => new THREE.CatmullRomCurve3(pts.map(([x, z]) => new THREE.Vector3(x, 0, z)), false, "centripetal");
const curve = toCurve(CONTROL);
export const HWY_LENGTH = curve.getLength();
const PTS = curve.getSpacedPoints(Math.ceil(HWY_LENGTH / STEP));

/** Unit tangents and right-hand vectors (world.js: right = (−fz, 0, fx)) for a sampled polyline. */
function frames(points) {
  const tan = [], right = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < points.length; i++) {
    const a = points[Math.max(0, i - 1)], b = points[Math.min(points.length - 1, i + 1)];
    const t = new THREE.Vector3(b.x - a.x, 0, b.z - a.z).normalize();
    tan.push(t);
    right.push(new THREE.Vector3(-t.z, 0, t.x));
  }
  return { tan, right };
}
const HWY = frames(PTS);

/** Nearest-sample distance for a polyline, through a coarse grid (good to ~STEP/2). */
function distanceField(points, cell = 24) {
  const buckets = new Map();
  points.forEach((p, i) => {
    const k = Math.floor(p.x / cell) + "," + Math.floor(p.z / cell);
    if (!buckets.has(k)) buckets.set(k, []);
    buckets.get(k).push(i);
  });
  return (x, z) => {
    const cx = Math.floor(x / cell), cz = Math.floor(z / cell);
    let best = Infinity;
    for (let dx = -1; dx <= 1; dx++) {
      for (let dz = -1; dz <= 1; dz++) {
        const list = buckets.get((cx + dx) + "," + (cz + dz));
        if (!list) continue;
        for (const i of list) best = Math.min(best, Math.hypot(points[i].x - x, points[i].z - z));
      }
    }
    return best;
  };
}
const hwyDistance = distanceField(PTS);
export const distanceToHighway = hwyDistance;
/** True on the carriageway (plus `pad` metres either side). */
export const onParishHighway = (x, z, pad = 0) => hwyDistance(x, z) < HWY_WIDTH / 2 + pad;

// the dirt road from the highway up to Bayou Noir and on past the fields
const DIRT_WIDTH = 6;
const DIRT_PTS = (() => {
  const c = toCurve([[-176, 47], [-205, 20], [-238, -8], [-262, -22], [-300, -38], [-334, -44]]);
  return c.getSpacedPoints(Math.ceil(c.getLength() / STEP));
})();
const DIRT = frames(DIRT_PTS);

r.d = r.z1 - r.z0; r.cx = (r.x0 + r.x1) / 2; r.cz = (r.z0 + r.z1) / 2;\n        if (r.w < 9 || r.d < 9) continue;                          // too small to be a building, and too small to matter\n        if (C.isFree(r)) out.push(r);\n      }\n      return out;\n    }\n    function lowRise(g, r, seed) {\n      const h = hash(r.cx, r.cz, 13);\n      if (h < 0.26 && r.w >= 16 && r.d >= 16) parts.garage(g, r.cx, r.cz, r.w, r.d, 2 + Math.floor(hash(r.cx, r.cz, 14) * 3), seed);\n      else if (h < 0.34) parts.tower(g, r.cx, r.cz, r.w - 2, r.d - 3, 16 + hash(r.cx, r.cz, 14) * 10, 2, seed);\n      else if (h < 0.68) parts.midrise(g, r.cx, r.cz, r.w - 1, r.d - 1, 11 + hash(r.cx, r.cz, 15) * 13, seed);\n      else if (r.w >= 15) {\n        // a terrace of Creole houses facing +z, and shotguns down the back\n        for (let x = r.x0 + 1; x < r.x1 - 4; x += 7) parts.creole(g, x + 3, r.z0 + 5, 6, 1, seed + x);\n        if (r.d >= 26) for (let x = r.x0 + 2; x < r.x1 - 3; x += 4) parts.shotgun(g, x, r.z1 - 10, -1, seed + x);\n      } else parts.midrise(g, r.cx, r.cz, r.w - 1, r.d - 1, 10 + hash(r.cx, r.cz, 15) * 9, seed);\n    }\n\n    let n = 0;\n    for (let i = 0; const TOWN = DISTRICTS.chatboro;
const wx = (x) => TOWN.x + x;
const wz = (z) => TOWN.z + z;
const wr = (r) => ({ x0: wx(r.x0), x1: wx(r.x1), z0: wz(r.z0), z1: wz(r.z1) });
const wp = (pts) => pts.map(([x, z]) => [wx(x), wz(z)]);

// ---- the plot ----
// Long along the highway and narrow across it, the way a highway village grows.
// 144 x 220 m: about half again the ground the old Chatboro end of the strip
// covered (~19,500 m2), and a fifth of the Tusouxroe metro (169,120 m2), which is
// the right ratio between a village and a city.
const BOUNDS = { x0: -96, x1: 48, z0: -120, z1: 100 };
const CORE = { x0: -90, x1: 42, z0: -114, z1: 94 };

// ---- the street plan ----
// US-167 and the Port Highway are laid by stateWorld.js as one plane each,
// running the length and breadth of the map. Chatboro marks their corridors on
// its own grid so nothing is built or planted on them, but it does NOT pave them
// again — `paved: false` is exactly that. The one exception is the Port
// Highway's western arm: stateWorld starts that road at x -6, which is the
// crossroads itself, so everything west of here is Chatboro's to surface.
// There is no street east of the highway. The first cut of this village had one
// — Mill Road — and it cost more than it gave: the east side is only forty
// metres deep, so Mill Road, the highway's own frontage and the three open areas
// were all fighting for the same strip, and two thirds of every frontage slot in
// the village was rejected for landing on something. Fourteen buildings came out
// of a plan for forty.
//
// A village of four thousand has ONE built-up side of the highway and fields on
// the other, which is both true of Chatham and what fits: the west side carries
// the streets, and the east side carries the gas station, the water tower and a
// pasture.
const MAIN_X = -44;           // Chatboro Main, one block west of the highway
const CHURCH_Z = -56;
const PINE_Z = 52;

/** The village water tower, in world space: prologue.js cuts to it at dawn. */
export const WATER_TOWER = { x: TOWN.x + 35, z: TOWN.z + 19 };

const STREETS = [
  { name: "Chatboro Main", points: [[MAIN_X, -110], [MAIN_X, 90]], width: 9, lampEvery: 36 },
  { name: "Church Street", points: [[-84, CHURCH_Z], [30, CHURCH_Z]], width: 8, lampEvery: 34 },
  { name: "Pine Street", points: [[-84, PINE_Z], [30, PINE_Z]], width: 8, lampEvery: 34 },
];

export function createChatboro(ctx) {
  const { scene } = ctx;
  const C = createComposer(ctx, {
    name: "Chatboro",
    bounds: wr(BOUNDS),
    zones: { core: wr(CORE), wild: wr(BOUNDS) },
    seed: 40831,
  });
  let announced = false;

  const std = (hex, rough, label, extra = {}) =>
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({ color: hex, roughness: rough, name: label, ...extra });

  function box(w, h, d, mat, x, y, z, ry = 0, parent = scene) {
    const m = new THREE.Mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(w, h, d), mat);
    m.position.set(x, y, z);
    m.rotation.y = ry;
    m.castShadow = m.receiveShadow = true;
    parent.add(m);
    return m;
  }
  /** World position of a point in a building's local frame (front = local +z). */
  const local = (slot, lx, lz) => [
    slot.x + Math.cos(slot.rot) * lx + Math.sin(slot.rot) * lz,
    slot.z - Math.sin(slot.rot) * lx + Math.cos(slot.rot) * lz,
  ];

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  // The houses. A village is mostly houses, and Lafourchette's shotgun house
  // (eastbank.js) is a city form — narrow, deep, built to a city lot. Up here
  // the lots are wide and cheap, so the house is a wide single-storey with a
  // hip roof and a porch across the front, which is what Jackson Parish
  // actually looks like.
  // -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  const SIDING = [0xe4d9c0, 0xb9c9b0, 0xd9c0b4, 0xc7d2dd, 0xefe8d8, 0xcfa88e, 0xaebd96];

  function buildSet() {
    // ---- 1 road: the crossroads, the village streets, and the plan --------
    // Both highways are already surfaced by stateWorld.js, so these two calls
    // only claim the ground. Paving them again would put a second plane a
    // millimetre above the first for 220 m.
    C.road("US-167", wp([[0, -118], [0, 98]]), { width: 12, paved: false, lampEvery: 44, sidewalk: 0 });
    C.road("Port Highway", wp([[0, 0], [46, 0]]), { width: 12, paved: false, sidewalk: 0 });
    // ...except its western arm, which stateWorld starts at the crossroads and
    // never lays. West of here the road is Chatboro's.
    C.road("Port Highway West", wp([[-94, 0], [0, 0]]), { width: 12, lampEvery: 40, y: 0.023 });
    for (const st of STREETS) {
      C.road(st.name, wp(st.points), { width: st.width, lampEvery: st.lampEvery || 0, y: 0.021 });
    }

    // Everything below is set clear of the corridors above, which are already on

    // West of Chatboro Main's own frontage band (x -61..-51), so the street can

````
## ✅ 2026-09-28 (Buffy): the Cathedral's steeples were floating in the sky

Human report, with photographs: "Cathedral seems ... cool" — and both shots show the same thing: the three steeples hovering detached above the building, with clear sky between the towers and the roof.

**It was a one-word bug in `nolalandmarks.js`:**

```js
mesh(new THREE.BoxGeometry(shaft, shaft, shaft), stucco, cx + x, 30 + height / 2, cz + z, ...)
```

`shaft` is the tower's **width**; the box's second argument is its **height**. So the "tower" was a CUBE of the width, while the spire above it was placed at `30 + height + height * 0.21` — on top of where a full-height shaft would have ended. Measured, after building the block: the central steeple's 11 m cube sat at y 55.5…66.5 under a spire starting at y 92, so **25.5 m of it did not exist**, and the two end steeples left 14.5 m gaps. The crosses and spires rendered fine, which is why nothing looked broken in a mesh count.

Fixed to `BoxGeometry(shaft, height, shaft)`. Centred at `30 + height / 2` it now spans exactly `30 … 30 + height` — the y the spire was already placed to sit on. The three shafts measure 30→92, 30→68, 30→68, each meeting its spire's base to the centimetre.

**Why every existing check passed anyway.** `landmarks_test.mjs` counted the three crosses and compared their heights ("the central steeple is much the tallest", 122 m vs 87 m) and measured the whole thing over 80 m tall. All true, all passing, with the towers in the air. **Counting cannot find a gap.** The new checks measure the *joint*: for each spire, find the shaft under the same x/z, and require that the shaft starts on the roofline and ends where the spire begins. Confirmed to fail 6 times against the old code and pass on the new, so it is a guard and not a decoration.

**Lesson worth carrying:** "it built three of the right things in the right places at the right relative heights" is not "it is one building". The invariant worth asserting is continuity — part A's top touches part B's bottom — because a missing *volume* between two correct, well-placed, correctly-sized parts is invisible to every count and to the whole silhouette test.

Committed. Not pushing — that's the deploy, and you haven't asked yet.

**What I found:** the empty space was real, but not where the last note assumed. It wasn't a missing grid row — it was Parish Highway 9 claiming a **74 m exclusion corridor around a 14 m road**, and the fallback for the blocks it touched cut each into three columns, which a *diagonal* road crosses in all three. Six of sixteen blocks came out completely empty.

**Metro now:**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| open ground (>30 m from a building) | 41.4% | **17.9%** |
| mean distance to a building | 35.2 m | **13.5 m** |
| mass per hectare | 40,207 | **59,600** |
| structures | 80 | **251** |
| tallest | 46 m | **69 m** |

The remaining 18% is US-167 and the highway — open because they're roads.

**I did not touch Chatboro, deliberately.** It measures **0% open ground** — every 20 m cell is within 30 m of a house. It's *thin* (19 buildings, 7.8 m tall), but that's what a village of 4,083 is, and its own source says so. I checked its 40 rejected building slots individually: every one is a legitimate junction refusal (a shop landing on the crossroads), not waste. Its mass/ha matching Metro's was a coincidence — reading that as "Chatboro is as empty as downtown" is exactly the trap the survey's two separate axes exist to prevent.

Two QA tools added: `landuse.mjs` (the survey) and `urban_density_test.mjs` (the guard, confirmed to fail 5/5 against the old code).

**One thing worth flagging:** extending the grid broke an existing test — it reported "-49 m clearance" on a grid where every street was correctly 7 m from everything. The check indexed blocks positionally against streets, which only works while every block sits between two streets. Rewrote it geometrically and added a "no block straddles a street" check, since clearance alone can't see a building standing in the road.

**Unverified:** there's no Chrome on this machine, so all of this is headless measurement of the scene graph. Whether the new low-rise infill actually *looks* like a city edge from the street is unconfirmed — worth a look when you next load it.

function buildGround() {
  ground = new THREE.Mesh(
    new THREE.PlaneGeometry(MAP.maxX - MAP.minX + WORLD * 0.4, MAP.maxZ - MAP.minZ + WORLD * 0.8, 1, 1),
    new THREE.MeshStandardMaterial({
      map: groundTexture(), color: 0x43552f, roughness: 1,
      // The floor is the player's depth reference. Applying the atmospheric fog
      // shader to this kilometre-scale plane made its near side blend into the
      // fog colour and look like a solid white/gray map.
      fog: false,
    })
  );
  ground.rotation.x = -Math.PI / 2;
  // centred on the grown map, and tiled to match its longer z so it doesn't stretch
  ground.position.x = (MAP.maxX + MAP.minX) / 2;
  ground.position.z = (MAP.maxZ + MAP.minZ) / 2;
  ground.material.map.repeat.set(30 * (MAP.maxX - MAP.minX + WORLD * 0.4) / (WORLD * 2.4),
                                 30 * (MAP.maxZ - MAP.minZ + WORLD * 0.8) / (WORLD * 2.4));
  ground.castShadow = false;
  scene.add(ground);
  realize(ground, { hint: "grass ground", shadows: false });
  ground.receiveShadow = true;
  // The derived maps inherit the albedo's repeat, which is what we want here,
  // but the relief needs dialling back at this tiling or it reads as gravel.
  ground.material.normalScale.set(0.6, 0.6);
}

const POOL_LIGHT_CAP = 30;
// Crown Strip interiors (crownStrip.js's `indoor: true` spots) don't have
// the outdoor problem this cap exists for — a casino floor isn't a bonfire a
// couple of metres from its own prop, it's a windowless room whose only light
// IS this fixture. Capped at 30 it read as pitch black except for chrome/neon
// accents that don't need a light at all (specular and emissive materials
// still show without one). Indoors gets a much higher knee instead.
const POOL_LIGHT_CAP_INDOOR = 55;
function updateLightPool(dt, focus) {
  poolTimer -= dt;
  if (poolTimer > 0 || !litSpots.length) return;
  poolTimer = 0.25;                       // 4 Hz is plenty for this
  for (const sp of litSpots) {
    sp.d = (sp.x - focus.x) ** 2 + (sp.z - focus.z) ** 2;
  }
  litSpots.sort((a, b) => a.d - b.d);
  for (let i = 0; i < lightPool.length; i++) {
    const l = lightPool[i];
    const sp = litSpots[i];
    // Parked at zero intensity rather than hidden: toggling .visible changes
    // the scene's light count, which recompiles every lit shader mid-frame.
    if (!sp || sp.d > 90 * 90) { l.intensity = 0; continue; }
    l.position.set(sp.x, sp.y, sp.z);
    l.color.setHex(sp.warm);
    l.distance = sp.range;
    // fade the outermost lights in rather than popping them on
    // Street lamps are accent lighting, not a second sun. Keep authored
    // interior/fire lights at full strength, but soften pooled lamp spill.
    // Every `power` here feeds a real, physically-decaying PointLight (decay 2,
    // set in initLightPool) with no minimum-distance floor, so a light placed a
    // couple of metres from its own prop (a sign, a torch, a bonfire — exactly
    // where most of these sit) blows that prop's surface to solid white and
    // bloom smears it across the frame; the sun itself never exceeds ~3.2
    // (daycycle.js), so a `power` of 16-170 is catastrophic up close no matter
    // how reasonable it looks from across the street. Soft-cap with a knee
    // (POOL_LIGHT_CAP) instead of a hard clamp: small fixtures barely move,
    // the worst offenders (klan bonfires, casino fronts) get pulled way down,
    // and every light keeps its authored ranking relative to the others.
    const cap = sp.indoor ? POOL_LIGHT_CAP_INDOOR : POOL_LIGHT_CAP;
    const nearFieldSafePower = cap * sp.power / (cap + sp.power);
    l.intensity = nearFieldSafePower * THREE.MathUtils.smoothstep(90 * 90 - sp.d, 0, 30 * 30) * (sp.fx === false ? 1 : lampPower * 0.72);
  }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------- collision registry

Committed. Not pushed — that's the deploy.

**I was wrong about what you're showing me.** These aren't empty spaces — the buildings are all there. I measured it with every district built (2,130 structures):

- distance to the nearest wall at the spawn point itself: **0 m**
- **100%** of ground within 50 m of spawn is within 30 m of a building
- **96%** within 200 m

What's actually wrong is **the lighting**. **91% of the ground in a 240 m box around spawn renders black at night**, with the buildings behind it lit. An unlit foreground reads as an empty one — that's why it looked like missing geometry.

**Three compounding faults, all measured:**

1. **The west side of the highway has no streetlamp at all.** Every lamp in the strip's run sits at `x = 0.5` — one kerb of a road spanning x −11…−1. Mean ground light west of the road: **0.000**. East: 0.101.
2. **Lamp spacing 22 m = lamp range 22 m.** The pools only touch at their exact midpoints, and with `decay: 2` the light there is **13% of peak**. Measured: ground falls to a third of peak between lamps.
3. **The light pool is hard-capped at 8 real point lights** for the whole state, and there are 671 litSpots. I simulated this on the real maths: 11 one-sided lamps → 93% black; alternating both sides → 92%; tightening spacing to 12 m → 91%. **No lamp arrangement fixes it**, because the constraint is how much ground 8 point lights can cover.

**I stopped short of fixing it, on purpose.** The real fix is raising the light pool cap, and that's a frame-time decision — this machine has no Chrome, so every number above is headless arithmetic, not a measured frame. Blowing the draw-call budget blind on a guess is how you make the game worse. It's written up in `TODO.md` with the three options and what each costs.

Two other things worth flagging:

- **My coverage metric was optimistic.** It measures distance to a building's *circumscribed circle*, which over-claims for long thin shapes (Metro has 38:1 buildings). Re-measured honestly, Metro is 19.2% open not 17.9% — my fix still stands — but OrleaRouge swings 39.5% → 79.3% on the same geometry. That metric needs an AABB.
- **I committed scratch files by accident.** Eight throwaway probes were tracked, three of them mine from this session via `git add -A`. Removed, and `.gitignore` now ignores `tools/qa/_*.mjs` so it stops recurring. My earlier density fix was never at risk.

This one **is** a real hole. Different defect from the lighting shots — that matters, so I measured it properly.

**The ground west of spawn, x −300..−100, z 140..340** — the exact block your screenshot is looking into:

| band | structures |
|---|---|
| x −300..−200 | **0** |
| x −200..−100 | **3** |
| x −100..0 | 4 |

That 200 × 200 m block you can ride straight through contains **one** structure, off to the side. The seam between Metro's south edge and OrleaRouge is **51% over 30 m from a wall**.

**Why it's empty** — and this one's a genuine bug, not a lighting illusion. `westparish.js` deliberately suppresses its own forest across Metro's box so the city owns that ground:

```js
// no forest in the city, only along the highway itself
if (x > -292 && x < -60 && z > -132 && z < 128 && !onParishHighway(x, z, 40)) return false;
```

That carve-out is a hard rectangle ending at **z = 128**. Spawn is **z = 130**. So everything west of the highway *south* of that line gets the worst of both: no trees (the carve-out killed them) and no city (Metro stops at 128). A dead grey plain with nothing in it, directly west of where you spawn.

**I stopped short of building it out, and I want to be straight about why.** There are two honest fixes — extend the city grid south past spawn, or widen the carve-out and let the roadside carry it — and which is right is a frame-time call. Spawn is the tightest spot in the state for draw calls, and **there's still no Chrome on this machine**, so I'd be adding geometry where it costs most with no way to measure the cost. That's the same reason I didn't touch the light pool.

Both findings are written up in `TODO.md` and committed. Still not pushed.

If you want, I can take the frame-time risk on this one — extending Metro south is a contained change and the measurement work is already done. Or if you'd rather see it first, say so and I'll push what exists so you can look at the current state in the browser.
